weaknesses: The headline claim of handling "any" or "arbitrary" NeRF architecture substantially exceeds the evidence. Combining a graph meta-network with rendering and cross-architecture contrastive objectives is coherent, and the proposed compact parameter graph for hash-table NeRFs is a concrete addition.

The study covers 13 configurations across MLP, tri-plane, and hash families, including several held-out hyperparameter variants. It evaluates classification and retrieval and includes useful comparisons among rendering-only, contrastive-only, and combined objectives.

Within the studied setting, the contrastive term provides clear evidence of improved cross-architecture transfer and retrieval relative to rendering-only training. The appendix also supplies many architectural, optimization, and hardware details.
weaknesses: The main multi-architecture claim lacks meaningful external baselines. Existing methods are simply marked inapplicable, but architecture-independent alternatives based on rendered views, sampled radiance-field outputs, family-specific encoders with alignment, or a directly supervised GMN are not evaluated. Consequently, the paper does not establish that its weight-space approach is competitive or that the proposed training design is necessary.

“Architecture-agnostic” and “unseen architecture” are overstated. Training covers all three evaluated families, while held-out models are only modest hyperparameter variations within those families. Generalization is brittle: LR+C obtains only 30.8% on TRI-8C and 27.8% on HASH-11T when the classifier is trained on ALL, despite these being within-family changes.

All quantitative experiments use one synthetic, object-centric ShapeNetRender dataset and simplified NeRFs without viewing-direction dependence. The Objaverse experiment is qualitative, apparently selectively illustrated, and uses the same MLP architecture as training; it therefore offers little evidence for generalization to new datasets, real scenes, or genuinely new architecture families.

The contrastive procedure assumes that every training object has been fitted independently with multiple NeRF architectures. These exact cross-architecture instance correspondences are expensive supervision and may rarely exist in realistic collections. The paper neither studies performance without such pairing nor adequately qualifies its “unsupervised” framing.

Retrieval remains weak in absolute terms: ALL/ALL Recall@1 is 5.3%, and several cross-family Recall@1 values are below 15%. There is no competitive retrieval baseline, chance-normalized analysis, or uncertainty estimate, making claims such as “robust” and “remarkable” difficult to support.

The evaluation reports no repeated runs, error bars, or statistical tests. This is especially problematic for claimed single-architecture improvements of roughly one percentage point. Important choices—including the loss weight, batch size of only eight for contrastive learning, graph features, pooling rule, and architecture mixture—receive no sensitivity analysis.

The hash-table graph omits the spatial hashing relationships that determine which 3D grid vertices access each table entry, retaining mainly table/entry identities and values. The paper does not establish that this representation preserves sufficient functional information, compare it with spatial alternatives, or analyze whether this omission explains the sharp HASH-11T degradation.

Classification uses a relatively powerful three-block nonlinear probe, so high accuracy does not by itself demonstrate a well-organized, architecture-invariant representation. Quantitative linear-probe or architecture-predictability measures would be more informative than the provided t-SNE plots.

The motivating efficiency argument is unevaluated: there are no inference-time, memory, parameter-count, or accuracy-versus-cost comparisons with render-based processing, while encoder training reportedly takes about two weeks on an RTX A6000. No code or newly generated NeRF dataset release is identified, further limiting reproducibility.

weaknesses: The central multi-architecture setting has no competitive baseline. Leaving nf2vec and Cardace et al. blank does not establish superiority over render-then-encode methods, architecture-specific ensembles, or alternative graph/set encoders trained with the same paired objective.

The claims of architecture-agnostic processing and generalization to unseen architectures are overstated. All unseen cases are hyperparameter changes within the same three templates; no genuinely unseen family, operator composition, or view-dependent NeRF is evaluated. Performance also collapses on changes such as TRI-8C and HASH-11T.

Evaluation is almost entirely confined to synthetic, standardized ShapeNetRender objects, with paired NeRFs trained from the same imagery. The Objaverse experiment is qualitative, extremely small, and uses an MLP architecture already seen during training, so it offers little evidence of dataset or real-world generalization.

Instance retrieval is weak in absolute terms—only 5.3% Recall@1 and 27.2% Recall@10 for ALL/ALL—and has no baseline, random-reference value, or uncertainty estimate. Showing semantically similar qualitative neighbors does not validate the stated exact-instance retrieval task.

The single-architecture improvements over prior methods are small and reported without multiple runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Moreover, when the classifier sees all architectures, the proposed combined objective performs worse than rendering-only training.

Evidence for architectural invariance is incomplete: t-SNE plots are qualitative and can be misleading, while no architecture-prediction probe, paired-distance metric, or controlled invariance analysis is provided.

Important ablations are missing, including the hash-graph design and its features, loss-weight sensitivity, embedding capacity, dependence on exact cross-architecture pairs, and scaling with graph size. The described hash graph also does not explicitly encode the coordinate-to-entry hashing rule or level resolutions, limiting support for general hash schemes.

Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of a stated code/data release, random-seed results, and some low-level sampling details, especially given the roughly two-week training time per principal model.

Several held-out configurations cause severe degradation, including 30.8% on TRI-8C and 27.8% on HASH-11T for LR+C with the classifier trained on ALL, compared with about 90% on the base architectures. Thus, even within-family robustness is uneven, contrary to some of the paper’s language.

Thus, the method is better characterized as paired self-supervision than fully unsupervised learning, and its data-generation cost limits scalability to arbitrary NeRF collections.
